# Surgery in the middle of a chain

You have a million records sitting in a dynamic array and you need to insert a new one between records 499,999 and 500,000. With the array from the last chapter you have to shift half a million elements over by one — a single `insert` call doing five hundred thousand writes. That's not a bug in your code. That's a property of contiguous storage: items next to each other in memory have to *stay* next to each other in memory, and the only way to make room in the middle is to push everything past it over.

A linked list answers that complaint with a completely different memory layout. Each element lives at its own address, wherever the allocator decided to put it, and each one holds a pointer to the next. Inserting an item in the middle rewrites exactly two pointers — regardless of how big the list is.

By the end of this chapter you'll have built singly linked, doubly linked, and circular linked lists, written the three textbook list-manipulation routines — *reverse*, *merge*, and Floyd's *tortoise-and-hare* cycle detection — and learned why a pointer is a different *kind* of address than an array index. The image to hold for the chapter is **pointer surgery**: every operation is a small, local rewrite of one or two pointers, never touching the rest of the chain. The price you pay for that locality is that you can no longer ask for the $i$-th element without walking $i$ steps to get there.

## A node knows its successor

A linked list isn't an object at the language level — it's a discipline you impose on a pile of small objects called **nodes**, each holding a value and a pointer to the next node. The end of the list is whichever node has its pointer set to `None`.

```python {export=src/codex/structures/linked.py}
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Iterator, Sequence
from codex.types import Ordering, default_order


@dataclass
class Node[T]:
    value: T
    next: "Node[T] | None" = None
```

The `next` annotation has to be a string because the class is referring to itself before its name has finished binding. That's a Python detail, not a deep one — every linked-structure language has some version of this footnote.

A *chain* of nodes is just a `Node[T]` you've decided to call the head. You don't need a separate list object to walk it. To iterate, you start at the head and follow `next` pointers until you hit `None`. To find the $i$-th element, you walk $i$ steps. To find the length, you walk the whole thing. Those last two are the linked-list tax: indexed access is $\Theta(i)$, not $O(1)$, and the structure can never compete with an array on workloads where you index a lot.

A typical chain laid out flat, with addresses standing in for "wherever each node ended up in memory":

```
 head ──▶ [3 | •]──▶ [1 | •]──▶ [4 | •]──▶ [1 | •]──▶ [5 | None]
        addr A     addr B     addr C     addr D     addr E
```

The addresses A through E might be anywhere in memory — no requirement of contiguity. The list as a whole holds together because each node's `next` pointer names the next address in the chain.

I'll also wrap a chain in a small `LinkedList[T]` class that tracks the head, the tail, and the size — so that operations like "append to the end" and "ask the length" can be $O(1)$ instead of $\Theta(n)$. Without the tail pointer, append has to walk the whole chain. With it, append is two pointer writes.

```python {export=src/codex/structures/linked.py}
class LinkedList[T]:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.head: Node[T] | None = None
        self.tail: Node[T] | None = None
        self._size = 0

    def __len__(self) -> int:
        return self._size

    def __iter__(self) -> Iterator[T]:
        cur = self.head
        while cur is not None:
            yield cur.value
            cur = cur.next
```

Iteration is the only operation that genuinely needs to touch every node, and it does so with a single walk. Everything else in the API is local.

## Insertion and deletion as pointer surgery

The four operations that actually exercise the data structure are prepend, append, insert-after, and delete-after. Each one rewrites a constant number of pointers; none of them touch nodes beyond their immediate neighbors. That's the chapter's recurring image made literal.

Prepend is the simplest: allocate a new node whose `next` points at the current head, then make that new node the head.

```python {export=src/codex/structures/linked.py}
    def prepend(self, value: T) -> None:
        node = Node(value, self.head)
        if self.head is None:
            self.tail = node
        self.head = node
        self._size += 1
```

The `self.head is None` check handles the empty case — the new node is *also* the tail when there was no tail before. That's the kind of edge case you have to think about exactly once when you write a linked list, and you trip on it every time you forget.

Append is the mirror image: allocate a new node, point the current tail's `next` at it, then make it the new tail.

```python {export=src/codex/structures/linked.py}
    def append(self, value: T) -> None:
        node = Node(value)
        if self.tail is None:
            self.head = node
        else:
            self.tail.next = node
        self.tail = node
        self._size += 1
```

Both are $O(1)$. That's the property the tail pointer buys you, and it's why every implementation of a linked list that wants to be taken seriously tracks the tail.

The two interesting operations are `insert_after` and `delete_after`. Both take a node handle — a reference to a specific node already in the list — and operate on its immediate neighborhood. They're the operations that demonstrate why linked lists exist.

```python {export=src/codex/structures/linked.py}
    def insert_after(self, node: Node[T], value: T) -> None:
        new_node = Node(value, node.next)
        node.next = new_node
        if node is self.tail:
            self.tail = new_node
        self._size += 1

    def delete_after(self, node: Node[T]) -> None:
        target = node.next
        if target is None:
            return
        node.next = target.next
        if target is self.tail:
            self.tail = node
        self._size -= 1
```

`insert_after` does two pointer writes: the new node's `next` gets the old successor, and the predecessor's `next` gets the new node. `delete_after` does one: the predecessor's `next` skips over the deleted target. Both are $O(1)$ — *given a handle to the node*. That "given a handle" qualifier is the silent caveat: if you have to find the node first by walking, you've paid $\Theta(n)$ before the surgery even started. Linked lists win when the caller already holds node handles — a pattern you'll meet again in chapter 11's deque and chapter 12's chained hash table.

Running the basic operations on a small example:

```{python}
from codex.structures.linked import LinkedList

chain = LinkedList[int]()
for x in [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]:
    chain.append(x)

print(list(chain))                       # [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] — appended in order
print(f"length: {len(chain)}")           # length: 5

chain.prepend(0)
print(list(chain))                       # [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5] — prepended at head

# Insert 99 after the node with value 2
node = chain.head
while node.value != 2:
    node = node.next
chain.insert_after(node, 99)
print(list(chain))                       # [0, 1, 2, 99, 3, 4, 5]
```

Notice the `while` loop walking to find the target node. That's the linked-list tax made visible: every operation on "the node with this value" pays a linear walk to find the node first. The $O(1)$ savings on `insert_after` itself doesn't change that. The structure is only really fast when something else gave you the handle.

## Reverse, in one pass

A classic interview problem, and the cleanest demonstration of pointer surgery in the chapter. Given the head of a chain, return the head of the same chain with every `next` pointer flipped.

The naive way is to walk the list, collect the values into an array, and rebuild a new list from the reversed array. That works, but it allocates $n$ extra nodes and copies every value — $O(n)$ time and $O(n)$ extra space, plus all the allocation churn. There's a cleverer way that does the work in place, with three pointers and no extra allocation.

The trick is to walk the chain with three pointers — `prev`, `cur`, and a saved-aside `nxt` — and at each step, flip `cur.next` to point backwards at `prev`, then advance both `prev` and `cur` by one step.

```python {export=src/codex/structures/linked.py}
def reverse[T](head: Node[T] | None) -> Node[T] | None:
    prev: Node[T] | None = None
    cur = head
    while cur is not None:
        nxt = cur.next
        cur.next = prev
        prev = cur
        cur = nxt
    return prev
```

Five lines, one walk, one node touched per step. The loop invariant: at the top of each iteration, the prefix of the chain from `head` to `prev` is already reversed, and `cur` points at the next node to flip. When the loop terminates, `cur` is `None`, the entire chain has been flipped, and `prev` is the new head — which is what the original tail used to be.

Let me run it.

```{python}
from codex.structures.linked import LinkedList, reverse

chain = LinkedList[int]()
for x in [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]:
    chain.append(x)

# reverse returns the new head; rebuild the iterable from it
new_head = reverse(chain.head)

values = []
cur = new_head
while cur is not None:
    values.append(cur.value)
    cur = cur.next
print(values)   # [5, 4, 3, 2, 1] — flipped, in place, with no new node allocations
```

Notice that `reverse` doesn't update the `LinkedList`'s head and tail attributes — it operates on the raw chain of nodes. If you wanted the wrapper class to stay consistent after a reverse, you'd write a method that calls `reverse(self.head)`, then swaps `self.head` and `self.tail`. I left that as a method-not-written so the algorithm itself stays small. The point is the surgery, not the bookkeeping.

## Merging two sorted lists

Merge sort's inner step from chapter 4 reappears here, but with one big difference: when the input is a linked list, you don't have to allocate a new array to hold the merged output. You can splice the existing nodes into a single sorted chain by walking two pointers, picking the smaller-headed node at each step, and threading it onto a growing result tail. Zero allocations beyond a single dummy node used to simplify the head case.

```python {export=src/codex/structures/linked.py}
def merge_sorted[T](
    a: Node[T] | None,
    b: Node[T] | None,
    order: Ordering[T] = default_order,
) -> Node[T] | None:
    dummy: Node[T] = Node(None)  # type: ignore[arg-type]
    tail = dummy
    while a is not None and b is not None:
        if order(a.value, b.value) <= 0:
            tail.next = a
            a = a.next
        else:
            tail.next = b
            b = b.next
        tail = tail.next  # type: ignore[assignment]
    tail.next = a if a is not None else b
    return dummy.next
```

The dummy node is the trick worth naming. Without it, you'd have to special-case the first iteration (when there's no existing tail to attach to). With the dummy, every iteration looks the same, and you return `dummy.next` at the end to skip past the placeholder. Its value is never read; the `# type: ignore` comments are the price of telling Python's type checker that a `None` placeholder is fine for `T`.

```{python}
from codex.structures.linked import LinkedList, merge_sorted


def to_chain(items):
    list = LinkedList[int]()
    for x in items:
        list.append(x)
    return list.head


def to_list(head):
    values = []
    cur = head
    while cur is not None:
        values.append(cur.value)
        cur = cur.next
    return values


a = to_chain([1, 3, 5, 7])
b = to_chain([2, 4, 6, 8])
merged = merge_sorted(a, b)
print(to_list(merged))   # [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8] — interleaved in sorted order

# Edge case: one side empty
print(to_list(merge_sorted(to_chain([1, 2, 3]), None)))    # [1, 2, 3]
print(to_list(merge_sorted(None, to_chain([4, 5, 6]))))    # [4, 5, 6]
```

This is the move that makes merge sort on linked lists *not allocate* during the merge step — a property functional-language sorts (Haskell, ML, Lisp) lean on hard. CPython's stable sort doesn't, because Python's `list` is an array.

## Tortoise and hare: detecting cycles

A linked list isn't supposed to have cycles — the convention is that the chain ends at a node whose `next` is `None`. But nothing in the language stops you from making `tail.next` point at an interior node, accidentally or deliberately, and any algorithm that walks the chain expecting `None` at the end will loop forever if there's a cycle.

Floyd's tortoise-and-hare algorithm detects cycles in $O(n)$ time and $O(1)$ space. Walk the chain with two pointers — a slow one advancing by one step per iteration, a fast one by two. If there's no cycle, the fast pointer hits `None` first and you're done. If there *is* a cycle, the fast pointer eventually catches up to the slow one from behind: both are running around the cycle, the fast one gaining one position per step, and the gap closes within $\lambda$ steps where $\lambda$ is the cycle length.

That meeting point isn't generally the *entry* to the cycle — it's some position inside it that depends on $\mu$ (head-to-entry distance) and $\lambda$. A second phase recovers the entry: reset one pointer to the head, advance both by one step at a time. The congruence $\mu + k \equiv 2(\mu + k) \pmod \lambda$ — worked out on paper — shows why they meet at the entry.

```python {export=src/codex/structures/linked.py}
def floyd_cycle[T](head: Node[T] | None) -> Node[T] | None:
    tortoise = hare = head
    while hare is not None and hare.next is not None:
        assert tortoise is not None  # tortoise is at most as far as hare
        tortoise = tortoise.next
        hare = hare.next.next
        if tortoise is hare:
            tortoise = head
            while tortoise is not hare:
                assert tortoise is not None and hare is not None
                tortoise = tortoise.next
                hare = hare.next
            return tortoise
    return None
```

The function returns the cycle's entry node, or `None` if there's no cycle. The two `assert`s are there to help Python's type checker — they're invariant claims about pointers, not runtime checks meant to catch bugs.

Let me build a chain with a deliberate cycle and verify Floyd finds the entry.

```{python}
from codex.structures.linked import LinkedList, floyd_cycle

# build a straight chain 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5 → 6 → 7
chain = LinkedList[int]()
for x in [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]:
    chain.append(x)

# locate the node with value 3
entry_target = chain.head
while entry_target.value != 3:
    entry_target = entry_target.next

# splice in a cycle: tail.next → node 3
# the chain becomes 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5 → 6 → 7 → 3 → 4 → 5 → 6 → 7 → 3 → ...
chain.tail.next = entry_target

entry = floyd_cycle(chain.head)
print(f"cycle entry: {entry.value}")   # cycle entry: 3 — Floyd found it

# and on a cycle-free chain, the algorithm returns None
clean = LinkedList[int]()
for x in [1, 2, 3]:
    clean.append(x)
print(floyd_cycle(clean.head))         # None — no cycle to find
```

The algorithm is constant-space — two pointers, no `visited` set — and linear-time, with at most $\mu + 2\lambda$ steps across both phases. The math underneath is the kind of result that looks like a coincidence until you've worked through it once, after which it never goes away.

## Doubly linked and circular variants

The singly linked list has one structural limitation: you can move forward but not backward. If you have a node handle and you want to delete *that* node, you can't — you'd need a handle to its predecessor, which the node itself doesn't know. That's why the API above is `delete_after`, not `delete`. The fix is to give each node a second pointer.

```python {export=src/codex/structures/linked.py}
@dataclass
class DoublyLinkedNode[T]:
    value: T
    prev: "DoublyLinkedNode[T] | None" = None
    next: "DoublyLinkedNode[T] | None" = None


def detach[T](node: DoublyLinkedNode[T]) -> None:
    if node.prev is not None:
        node.prev.next = node.next
    if node.next is not None:
        node.next.prev = node.prev
    node.prev = None
    node.next = None
```

`detach` removes a node from its chain in $O(1)$ given only the node's own handle — the operation singly linked lists fundamentally cannot do. That property is what makes the doubly linked list the natural backbone for chapter 11's deque, for LRU caches, and for any structure that holds external handles and wants deletion to be local.

The cost is one extra pointer per node and one extra rewrite per operation. Memory roughly doubles; whether that's a fair trade depends on the workload.

The circular variant is a chain whose tail's `next` points back at the head, so there's no `None` at the end. It's what `floyd_cycle` treats as a bug, except deliberately. Useful for round-robin schedulers, certain kinds of buffers, and some auxiliary graph-algorithm structures in Part V. The construction is one line of post-processing.

```python {export=src/codex/structures/linked.py}
def make_circular[T](head: Node[T] | None) -> Node[T] | None:
    if head is None:
        return None
    cur = head
    while cur.next is not None:
        cur = cur.next
    cur.next = head
    return head
```

And you'd walk one of these with a counter, not a `while cur is not None`, because the loop condition would never fire. That's the whole structural change — the rest of the code that operates on chains carries over unchanged.

## The three questions, applied

You've now built three flavors of linked list and three textbook routines that operate on them. Time for the three questions, applied to the structure as a whole.

### Is it correct?

The invariants of the singly linked `LinkedList` class are three. First: if `head` is `None`, then `tail` is `None` and `_size` is 0 — the empty case is unambiguous. Second: if `head` is not `None`, then `tail` is the unique node reachable from `head` by following `next` pointers whose own `next` is `None` — the chain terminates exactly once. Third: `_size` equals the number of nodes reachable from `head`. Each operation preserves all three; the edge cases (empty list, single node, deletion of the tail) are the places you have to think carefully, which is why the body of every method has at least one branch handling them.

The standalone functions are simpler. `reverse` is correct by its loop invariant: at iteration $i$, the first $i$ nodes have been flipped, and `cur` points at the next node to flip. `merge_sorted` is correct because at every step, the chosen node is the smallest available from either input — the same exchange argument that proves merge sort's merge step correct, transferred from arrays to chains. `floyd_cycle` is correct because of the cycle-length congruence: if a cycle exists, the two pointers must eventually meet inside it, and the second-phase walk lands at the entry by the modular-arithmetic identity.

### How efficient is it?

The per-operation cost table for the singly linked `LinkedList`:

| Operation | Cost | Why |
|-----------|------|-----|
| `prepend`, `append` | $O(1)$ | Two pointer writes, with the tail pointer available. |
| `insert_after(node, x)`, `delete_after(node)` | $O(1)$ | Two pointer rewrites given a node handle. |
| Find by value | $\Theta(n)$ | Walk the chain. |
| Find by index | $\Theta(i)$ | Walk $i$ steps from the head. |
| `__len__` | $O(1)$ | Maintained as an attribute. |
| `__iter__` | $\Theta(n)$ | One walk through the chain. |

The standalone routines: `reverse` is $\Theta(n)$ time, $O(1)$ space. `merge_sorted` is $\Theta(n + m)$ time, $O(1)$ space. `floyd_cycle` is $\Theta(n)$ time, $O(1)$ space — with the explicit constant at most $\mu + 2\lambda$ for a chain with cycle. Space across the structure as a whole is $\Theta(n)$, with the constant above 1 per element because each node holds a pointer plus a value. Doubly linked variants double that pointer overhead.

### Is it optimal?

For the operations a linked list is designed to make cheap, yes. Insert and delete given a handle to the predecessor are $\Omega(1)$ — you have to write at least one pointer — and the linked list hits that bound. Reverse is $\Omega(n)$ because every position changes. Cycle detection is $\Omega(n)$ because the cycle might be anywhere in the chain.

For the operations a linked list makes expensive, no — and that's exactly the trade. Random access at $\Theta(i)$ instead of $O(1)$ is the cost of giving up contiguous storage. An array can do better; a linked list fundamentally cannot. Workload decides: index-heavy callers reach for arrays, insertion-heavy callers holding node handles reach for linked lists, and most real software ends up needing some of both.

## What linked structures teach you

The singly linked list is correct by three invariants — head, tail, size — and makes prepend, append, and adjacent insert/delete $O(1)$ given handles, at the cost of $\Theta(i)$ random access. The doubly linked variant doubles the pointer cost in exchange for $O(1)$ detach-by-handle, which makes it the backbone of every structure that holds external handles and needs to delete by them. The circular variant is a one-line transformation that turns the chain into a loop.

The lesson worth carrying forward is that a pointer is a *different kind of address* than an integer index. An array index is a logical position relative to a base; recomputing it is free. A pointer is a physical address that's only useful given the pointer itself; recomputing it from a logical position requires walking. That difference is the source of every asymptotic asymmetry between arrays and linked lists.

Now that you have both contiguous and linked storage, the next two chapters introduce disciplines — restrictions on the operations you allow — that make these structures behave like something more than themselves. A stack restricts you to one end of the sequence; a queue restricts you to one end for input and the other for output. The implementations are short, because the structures from this chapter and the last do the heavy lifting. What those restrictions *buy* you is the interesting part.

## Notes and further reading

The singly and doubly linked list constructions are CLRS (4th ed.) §10.2 and Sedgewick & Wayne's *Algorithms* (4th ed.) §1.3. Floyd's tortoise-and-hare algorithm is folklore by 1970 but is most often attributed to Robert Floyd, with the formal exposition appearing in Knuth's *The Art of Computer Programming* Vol. 2 §3.1 exercises. The modular-arithmetic proof of the entry-point recovery step is worked out in detail in CLRS Problem 10-2. The in-place linked-list reversal is sometimes called "the three-pointer dance" and shows up in essentially every coding-interview compendium. Brian Kernighan's *Practice of Programming* §2 has a memorable discussion of the dummy-node trick for merge-style routines, including a defense of why the trick is worth the slightly weird-looking allocation.
